svg.text: Multi-Cloud — GCP compute, Azure data (constraint-driven)
This split is only justified by a hard constraint (data residency / org mandate). The red cross-cloud hop is the cost + latency you're accepting — name it, don't hide it.
main.tf — ONE Terraform config, TWO providers: `google` (GKE, GLB, Apigee) + `azurerm` (Postgres, Redis, Event Hubs, Entra ID)

Terraform doesn't make the clouds interchangeable — it gives you one workflow, one state, one review process across both. The cross-cloud link (VPN/interconnect), the workload-identity federation, the firewall rules — all version-controlled here.
Latency floor (physics — can't be configured away):
same-region cross-cloud ~1–5ms (a tax you absorb) · cross-REGION 10–100ms+ (felt on every call — avoid) · so co-locate compute + data in ONE region even when clouds differ.
The reframe: you don't "optimise" the hop — you MINIMISE how many there are and make the unavoidable ones asynchronous.

GCP-side cache — Memorystore (Redis), co-located with compute
cache-aside for hot reads → turns N cross-cloud DB reads into ~0. Data locality is the #1 latency tool.
Workload Identity Federation (cross-cloud auth mechanism)
GKE service account → federates to Entra ID → gets a SHORT-LIVED Azure token.
No Azure secret stored in GCP — this is what makes "auth by Entra ID" work across clouds.
Deploy: GitOps (ArgoCD) → GKE
signed image from Artifact Registry · admission control · canary. Code ships to GKE only; Azure data tier is managed PaaS (no deploy).
Cross-cloud bridge — GCP Cloud VPN / Partner Interconnect
ALL cross-cloud traffic funnels through here. Private encrypted path; non-overlapping CIDR required.
Interconnect (not internet VPN) for a bank — predictable, SLA-backed latency, no public transit.
The 3 ways to bridge two clouds (pick by volume + sensitivity)
A · Public endpoint + mTLS + IP allowlist
internet path, variable latency, cheapest, minutes to set up.
Low-volume / non-sensitive only. Not for a bank moving real data.
B · Site-to-site VPN (IPsec)
private routing over internet backbone, throughput CAPPED per tunnel,
hours to set up. The cost-sensitive middle ground.
C · Dedicated interconnect (Partner Interconnect ↔ ExpressRoute)
off the public internet, lowest + PREDICTABLE latency, SLA-backed, high
throughput. Weeks to provision, most expensive. The bank answer.
CROSS-CLOUD HOP — egress $ + latency, every call

Azure Event Hubs (Kafka surface)
async event backbone — saga events, outbox→CDC
publishes here. Async tolerates the cross-cloud hop.
All data + identity is residency-bound to Azure —
the reason compute-in-GCP has to reach across.
auth (federated)
DB queries (sync — minimise)
events (async — tolerant)
How to defend this design (and when NOT to)
1 · Lead with honesty: this split is a constraint, not a preference.
"I'd only put compute in GCP and data in Azure if a hard constraint forced it — residency law, or an org mandate. Left to choose I co-locate them,
because every cross-cloud call costs egress and adds latency. And I don't optimise the hop — I minimise hop count and make the rest async."
2 · The bridge is the crux — private IPs don't route across clouds by themselves.
A VPN or Partner Interconnect/ExpressRoute connects the networks first; only then does private DB access work. First constraint: non-overlapping CIDR.
For a bank, dedicated interconnect over internet VPN — predictable SLA-backed latency, no public transit.
3 · Cross-cloud auth = workload identity federation, never a stored secret.
GKE service account federates to Entra ID for a short-lived token. A static Azure credential in GCP is what a security review fails you for.
Network gets you connected; federated identity gets you authenticated.
4 · Mitigate the latency you can't remove — cache LOCAL, cross async.
Hot read-cache on the GCP side (Memorystore), not across the hop — caching in the other cloud defeats the cache. Batch cross-cloud calls, keep
chatty sync DB reads out of the hot path, push work onto the async Event Hubs path which tolerates the latency far better than sync reads.
One main.tf, two providers, one workflow. Red arrows = the price of the constraint. An architect names that price rather than pretending it's free.
